title: AI is heading toward a cash-flow negative inflection point, and spending will slow in 2027, Wall Street thinks
source_used: Fortune (AI section of the Fortune Daily newsletter)
key_facts: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of Columbia Business School estimates that capital spending will surpass the combined operating cash flow of Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet for the first time in 2026.
His paper says internal cash is no longer enough to fund the projected pace of investment without more outside capital.
Wells Fargo analysts expect the market to start thinking about 2027 as a potential peak year for AI capex, and say most investors agree capex will likely slow meaningfully in 2028.
Pantheon Macroeconomics expects hyperscaler capex growth to moderate in 2027, with chip, power and labour bottlenecks and higher borrowing costs increasingly biting.
Pantheon expects AI-linked investment to keep growing very strongly, and says higher borrowing costs are unlikely to derail the buildout while financing stays readily available.
Fortune's own framing: spending growth is set to slow as financing gets tighter.
quote_evidence: On current estimates, capex will surpass the five firms' combined operating cash flow for the first time in 2026.

Internal cash generation remains substantial, but it is no longer sufficient to finance the projected pace of investment without greater reliance on external capital or financing structures that shift assets and obligations away from the operating companies' balance sheets.
But they are unlikely to derail the buildout while financing remains readily available and the largest tech firms continue to expect exceptionally high returns from AI.
why_it_matters_hint: Big tech may need more outside money for AI buildout; analysts forecast slower capex growth in 2027, but say the buildout continues.
notes: Read in full. The Fortune text is a daily newsletter; only the AI paragraphs (capex, cash flow, analyst views) are used. The 'five firms' are the names the article gives in brackets (Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Alphabet). The 'Wall Street thinks' framing is the headline's; the analysts are named by firm only.
